copy_pick.why: Its 'KREMLIN PLOTS A POLISH FRAME-UP' blurb is the shortest and punchiest take on the tabloid directive, and it is the only summary that skips the 'Meanwhile' crutch the recent cards lean on, closing with a sharp photo-op-versus-everything-else line.

doom.driver: Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine.
doom.summary: While Trump, Xi and Putin swapped 'my friend' handshakes in Shenzhen, reports surfaced that Moscow had sketched a mass-casualty attack in Poland with Ukraine's name pre-printed on the blame. Iran is lobbing missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain again, Nginx has a hole big enough to drive the internet through, and Anthropic just raised $81 billion, presumably to buy a very large fire extinguisher. Diplomacy is having a lovely photo op. Everything else is not.

factors.name: AI Capability
factors.detail: Gemini 4 Neon, Microsoft's seven new models and a 385x efficiency claim made it a crowded day at the frontier.

factors.name: Governance
factors.detail: Nvidia's China chip scandal reached the White House just as Trump declared America the superintelligence champ.

factors.name: Geopolitics
factors.detail: Iran is striking Gulf states after a US hit on Qeshm, Houthis are aiming at Riyadh, and a Russian false-flag plot targeted Poland.

factors.name: Alignment
factors.detail: The frontier AI pause is quietly gone, and Meta's Muse is hallucinating people's bank balances.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: Battlefield lasers and a Musk-Zelenskyy spat add flavor, not catastrophe.

doom.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. Extreme close-up on a single paper poster pasted to a weathered red-brick Gothic gable wall in a Warmian-Masurian border town. The poster fills the frame. Only the edges show the setting: the brick courses with white lime mortar, and at the lower right a red-and-white striped border post. At the lower left, coils of razor wire glint on a steel fence. A furnace-orange floodlight on the ground blasts hard light up the wall, so every brick glows rust-red and the cast shadows are bruised violet. A thick blood-red fog hangs behind the wire. The poster is a lurid theatrical illustration: heavy crimson stage curtains drawn apart on a cramped toy stage. The tall pale wooden Gleiwitz radio tower stands on the stage, a lattice of slats drawn in glowing orange, with its shadow stretching across the painted floor. A blue-and-yellow cloth patch hangs on a tiny hook in the center of the stage, the one clean saturated blue-yellow spot in the picture, shining like bait. Painted strings run from above the stage to the patch and to a row of small flat cut-out figures in Polish-style uniforms. The figures are drawn whole, in a line, like stage props. The poster is torn and curling at its corners, its lower half peeling away from the brick. A glossy wet streak of rain runs down it, mirroring a flicker of blue police light in the puddled ground at the bottom edge. The scene is bright, hellish and malevolent, with crisp pixel clusters, dithered orange glow and clear shapes readable at phone size.

minor: The six cut-out figures are nearly identical and their faces are small and indistinct, as expected for flat stage props.
The strings above the figures are faint and do not clearly attach to each figure or to the flag.
The razor wire at the lower left is mostly a dark silhouette and reads as an odd trident or fork shape.
The blue-yellow flag has no visible hook except a small bracket, and the hanging strings look a little tangled.
The poster edge and the torn bottom corners blend into the brick, so the paper reads as slightly fused with the wall.
The floodlight at the lower left is a blurry glowing block.
The blue rain streak at the bottom is faint, and no blue police light is clearly visible.

dawn.driver: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details.
dawn.blurb: ONE LIGHT-DAY OUT, STILL CARRYING SONGS
dawn.summary: Forty-nine years after leaving Earth with a golden record of music and greetings, Voyager 1 is now so far away that its signals take a full day to reach us. It is the most distant object humans have ever made, and a historian is revisiting the record's forgotten details, which its makers expect to last a very long time. Closer to home, researchers found that a rare inflammatory disorder in infants may respond to medicines that already exist, and one baby is already improving.

factors.name: Science
factors.detail: Physicists found that electrons can form stable pairs at room temperature, a key step toward electricity that flows without resistance.

factors.name: Cooperation
factors.detail: New Scientist celebrates 70 years of bringing discoveries from labs around the world to curious readers.

factors.name: Human Spirit
factors.detail: A family dog in England kept nudging at a baby boy, which led his mother to discover a heart condition early enough to get him care.

factors.name: Environment
factors.detail: Scientists built a rechargeable battery around vitamin B12 that lasted 250 charging cycles, pointing toward greener alternatives to lithium-ion.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: Researchers filmed the rare barreleye fish in 4K, showing its see-through head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet down.

dawn.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. SILHOUETTE COMPOSITION in the deep interstellar dark one light-day from home. The environment fills the frame: a vast vertical gradient sky glows like clean morning light, with soft sage green at the top melting into warm amber and pale honey-gold at the horizon-like center. The effect is dawn at the edge of the solar system, shadows lifting and clarity arriving. A tiny, blazing Sun sits low on the left as a bright cream-white pixel cluster with a few stepped, dithered rings of amber and pale green haze. Sparse stars glint through the upper green, and a few faint dust bands drift across the glow. VOYAGER 1 floats in the lower right third as a crisp, near-black silhouette against the light. It has a large round high-gain dish antenna in profile, a long thin magnetometer boom stretching diagonally, the angular bus with a scan platform, and a skeletal RTG boom. The Golden Record cover is mounted on the bus and turned half toward us. Its gold-plated face catches the backlight with a bright burnished-gold rim and a few warm highlight pixels, and tiny etched pulsar-map lines and hieroglyph-style marks glint on its surface, with a second pristine set of engravings just visible along the inner edge of the open cover. A thin dotted line of amber signal pixels runs from the dish back across the glow toward a minuscule blue-green Earth dot near the Sun. The scene is calm, patient and tender, with strong contrast between the dark probe and the luminous sky, and no people or text.

minor: The Voyager silhouette is a bit jumbled around the bus. The golden record disc and a second round disc behind it overlap, and the legs and struts beneath are tangled. It still reads as a probe.
The boom on the right ends in clustered blobs that don't clearly match real instruments. Most viewers will take it as stylized detail.
The dotted signal line starts at the dish edge, not clearly from the dish center. It also fades out before reaching the tiny Earth dot, so the link is faint.
The golden record's etched marks are only vague smudges at phone size. This is acceptable given the pixelation.
